the predominantly wooden buildings, especially on the outskirts of the town, including barns and stables, posed a fire hazard that was difficult to control. At the end of 1821, another massive fire ravaged the town. As many as 16 houses, 62 barns, 2 granaries, 2 stables and 13 sheds burnt down in the peas- ant suburb and along the road to reszel (today’s Powstańców Warszawy Street). the losses were estimated at 24,532 thalers. In order to avoid fires with such disastrous consequences in the future, the decision was made to separate the farm and residential buildings from the flammable barns. Hence, a single street named Neue Sorge was originally laid out especially for barns. It encompassed the areas on today’s Ignacego Daszyńskiego, Powstańców Warszawy and Mazurska Streets. Further streets, along which barns were built, were delineated later – today’s Ignacego Daszyńskiego (up to Powstańców Warszawy Street), Adama Mickiewicza, Juliusza Słowackiego and Wilcza Streets. Nonetheless, the clustering of warehouse buildings along designated streets did not shield the town from fires. In 1860, fire consumed Louis Kolmar’s new mill buildings, the edifices of the old municipal hospital and many residential houses in Castle Liberty. Another great fire in one of the delimited barn-built streets (today’s Adama Mickiewicza Street) in 1890 engulfed 20 buildings, including two residential ones. the burnt-down area was reused as a site for the district starosty hall built in 1895. During the 1900 fire in former Peasant Suburb, ten buildings were damaged. In the attic of the town hall, which burned down at the time, part of the municipal archive got destroyed114 the town’s auspicious development was halted by the onset of the First World War. In August 1914, large areas of East Prussia were occupied by the russian troops of the 1st “Niemen” army of general rennenkampf and the 2nd “Narew” army of general Samsonov. russian soldiers entered Kętrzyn on August 25th. on August 30th, russians blew up the signal box, locomotive depot, cargo warehouses and bridge of the narrow-gauge railway, set fire to the coal depot at the railway station, buildings on Charlottenberg and outbuildings of the infirmary. they also tried to blow up the railway bridge over the Guber. three days later, on September 2nd, the officers’ mess at the grenadier barracks was burnt down. on the eve of the withdrawal from the town, on September 3rd, russians abducted Mayor Wilhelm Pieper and imprisoned him in their camp in Biedaszki. they forced the inhabitants to pay a contribution of 22,000 marks in an hour and a half115

In the second half of the 19th c., large industrial plants began to emerge in the town, providing permanent and seasonal employment, contributing to the prosperity of the inhabitants, and contributing to the development of smaller plants focused on servicing the local population. After 1818, the former fulling mill was converted into a mill, known as the “lower mill”. In the 19th c., the town’s landscape featured windmills, which were erected in the area of the current stadium and on the road to ryn (today’s ogrodowa Street). the windmill by the road to ryn operated for the longest period, even into the 1930s. In 1848, Louis Kolmar bought the former castle mill and started to expand it, and in 1859 he installed a steam drive in the mill. As he purchased the “lower mill” in 1874, he laid the foundations for the mill works (rastenburger Mühlenwerke) established after 1903 by Adolf Gramberg. In the 1880s other large factories commenced operations: a brewery in the former Węgorzewo Suburb and Wilke’s yeast factory near the castle. In 1881, a municipal slaughterhouse was built on the Neue Sorge. In Kętrzyn, right after the war ended, the Soldiers’ and Workers’ Council remained active for three months. the Council’s brief existence and the predominance of soldiers in its composition meant that its activities did not assume a revolutionary character, as was the case in larger cities. Soon after the end of the war, the war damage to the province, the sense of defeat and the rising costs of living and unemployment rate led to an increase in social discontent. In Kętrzyn this was particularly sharply manifested in the anti-Jewish riots that took place on May 22nd, 1919. Several hundred participants of the Social Democrats’ rally set out to march through the town after holding a meeting, which ended with looting and devastation of the shops of Jewish merchants132 132 J. D-354-MK) Despite the post-war crisis, the municipal infrastructure was continuously modernised. In 1933, the E. Bieske company from Königsberg installed a new pump and filter station in Jeżewo (Jeesau). For more than 90 years it was the only water intake for the town. Between 1927 and 1928, the specialist company Windschild & Langelott from Königsberg rebuilt the town’s sewage treatment plant as the need to modernise it arised. this plant was in operation for more than 60 years. Between 1924 and 1925, the Elektro-Bau-union company built the first power plant in Kętrzyn consisting of two transformer units (present ogrodowa Street). Due to increasing demand for electricity, a third transformer was built in 1928137 Considerable financial resources were allocated by the town and district authorities for new school and hospital buildings. In 1927, a new edifice for the primary school, Hippelschule (now Primary School No. 1), was opened on Bismarck Street (now Mikołaja Kopernika Street); the school was based on the boys’ school (Germ. Knabenschule), formerly a suburban primary schools (founded 1829). In 1930, another new school building for female students of the Hindenburg High School (now Middle School No. 1) was ceremonially opened on Deutschordenstraße (now Wojska Polskiego Street)138. In 1928, the District Mental Health Care was built in the former Georgenthal to a design by H. Stoffregen. In 1930, another wing was added to the older district hospital building, which, besides space for 40 beds, contained rooms for physical therapy, a laboratory, and numerous staff offices. By the mid-1930s, the hospital had 180 beds. In 1934, the municipal swimming pool was opened and the old swimming pool on the lake was demolished. 1937 saw the open- 137 Städtische Betriebswerke (as n. 113), pp. 158–160. 138 t. Korowaj, Rastenburg/Kętrzyn (as n. 69), pp. 219–220. ing of the sports hall and stadium of the rastenburger Sport Verein, built on former Castle Liberty, on the hill above the Guber, opposite St. George’s Church139 In the interwar period, Kętrzyn maintained its status of a garrison town. After the end of hostilities, the Grenadier regiment returned to the town from the Western Front on January 1st, 1919, followed by the Artillery regiment ten days later. under the treaty of Versailles, the both regiments were disbanded. A Grenadier Battalion of the 2nd (Prussian) Infantry regiment was deployed in the barracks vacated by the 4th Grenadier regiment. Part of the infantry barracks was converted into apartments. In order to maintain the garrison in the town, the infantry barracks with the officers’ mess were sold by the town to the state on July 1st, 1923, for 400 million marks, which was not a high sum given the high inflation rate at the time. From 1920 to 1927, the artillery barracks housed the security police. From January 1st, 1928, these buildings were handed over to the town, which began to convert them into apartments. It was not until 1934 that the town sold the artillery barracks to the state for 900 thousand marks140. After 1933, the Nazi authorities deployed the headquarters and two battalions of the newly formed 23rd Infantry regiment, as well as a division of the 11th Artillery regiment, in the town.

At the wartime field cemetery on Elisenhöhe near the infirmary, along the road to reszel, a memorial designed by Heinz Stoffregen from Bremen was then unveiled in memory of the 1,330 inhabitants of the district who had fallen during the First World War, as well as soldiers from the Grenadier regiment and the Field Artillery regiment. the memorial was made by the local construction company of Martin Modricker. the field cemetery is the final resting place of 336 soldiers (including 75 russian, 2 French and 1 romanian)141 During the interwar period, the population slowly grew despite the crisis of the 1920s. In 1919, Kętrzyn was inhabited by 12,320 people. twenty years later, there were 19,634 inhabitants in the town142. the destruction of the province during the First World War and the postwar crisis did not induce changes in the town’s economy. Kętrzyn retained the character of a town with large processing industry plants (sugar factory, grain mills, brewery, yeast factory) and a large number of craft enterprises of varying scale. An important element that characterised Kętrzyn at that time were numerous schools educating young people from the region, and the well-developed network of railway connections, numerous hotels, inns and guesthouses. After the German army invaded France, in April 1940, Germans started to construct a heavily fortified bunker complex in the forest near Gierłoż, intended as a wartime headquarters for Hitler and the German General Staff. In Kętrzyn, near the sugar factory buildings, a special office of the todt organisation was set up to manage the bunker construction, disguised under the meaningless name Chemische Werke Askania. In autumn 1944, as the eastern front approached, anti-tank entrenchments began to be dug near the town. When the onslaught of russian troops began across the eastern front on January 12th, 1945, no evacuation permit had yet been issued for the civilian population in the town. the order to evacuate did not come until the afternoon of January the 26th, when russian troops were already crossing the line of the Great Masurian Lakes. In a panicky and disorderly escape, not everyone managed to leave the town. At the Linden Market, the retreating German troops blew up the reserve ammunition. they also destroyed the railway bridge over the Guber, the power station and the town’s waterworks. russian troops entered the town on January the 27th at around 9am and seized it without a single shot being fired. It was then that the period of unjustifiable rapes and murders of civilians, looting and mindless destruction of the town by russians began. Wartime destruction and the post-war deportation of surviving machinery and equipment forced the Polish authorities to rebuild the town’s existing industrial plants. the agricultural character of the region influenced the development of the pro- cessing industry and agricultural services. the first agricultural processing plants – the brewery, sugar factory, mill, distillery and tannery – were put into operation already in 1945. the following year, a coffee roasting plant and the yeast factory were opened. In 1948, a dairy joined the ranks. In addition to the factories related to agriculture that had been operating in the town before 1945, other industrial sectors were also established in the town. Already in 1948, the “Styl” company was established for wood processing and the production of Christmas tree ornaments. A year later, sports industry company started its production activity; in 1958, it was divided into the “Warmia” clothing industry company and the “K-16” cable equipment factory. the latter would eventually became the “Farel” electro-technical equipment factory. the top-down imposition of industrialisation gave rise to at times bizarre ideas, such as the project to situate the clothing industry company “Warmia” in the buildings and stables of the stallion herd152. After 1989, some of the privatised enterprises were closed down (e.g. brewery, sugar factory, yeast factory, cereal factory). the now privately owned “Warmia” company, “Farel” taken over by the Dutch “Philips”, and the Cooperative “Styl” purchased by “MtI” have continued to develop. 151 Rocznik statystyczny powiatu Kętrzyn (as n. 149), p. 24–25; Rocznik statystyczny województwa olsztyńskiego (as n. 149), p. 43, 47; Powierzchnia i ludność w przekroju terytorialnym – 2004, Tablice, tab. 26 – https://stat.gov.pl/cps/rde/xbcr/gus/ powierzchnia_ludnosc_teryt_2004.zip (accessed: 20.11.2022); Powierzchnia i ludność w przekroju terytorialnym w 2016, Warszawa 2016, p. 145. 152 T swat, Dzieje Kętrzyna (as n. 144), pp. 100–103, 108–109; Z. At the end of the 20th c., during the period of political transformation, the economy of

the region changed. Following the rapid collapse of agricultural production (which to that point had been dominated by state farms), businesses operating as agricultural service companies had also, ceased their activities. After years of crisis, a number of new service and commercial companies operating in the local and regional market emerged in the town, usually replacing the factories that had existed before.
